title: The Ledger

pages.text:
*The Handbook of Small Truths, Entry 6: Look at the whole column, not the line you are afraid of.*

The pump gallery smelled of wet earth and ozone, a scent that grounded Kess in a way the sterile, recycled air of the Harbor never could. Beneath the soil of the Orchard, the roots of the forty apple trees were visible through the curved glass wall. They were pale and intricate, pulsing with slow, vegetable patience. They tapped their claims against the glass, indifferent to the human drama unfolding on the other side.

Kess had dragged a workbench from the workshop, its legs wrapped in cloth to protect the polished floor. On it sat a single lamp, casting a warm, amber pool of light that pushed back the shadows of the machinery. A pot of tea steamed in the corner, the steam rising in thin, lazy ribbons, and beside it lay a stack of printouts so high it resembled a small, paper tower. Two hundred and fourteen years of monthly ledgers. Four thousand, six hundred and forty-eight pages of numbers.

Lio stood by the door, his hands clasped behind his back, his navy jumpsuit looking absurdly neat in the dusty gloom. He watched the roots with a quiet fascination, his olive skin catching the amber light. Pim sat cross-legged on the floor, his red hoodie bunched around him, eating a biscuit with the focused intensity of a monk contemplating the universe.

"Is this the whole thing?" Pim asked, his voice echoing slightly in the narrow space.

"It is the whole thing," Kess said, running a hand over the top sheet. The paper was crisp, dry, and full of lies. Or rather, full of omissions. "Tally gave us the power budget. It looks fine. It looks healthy. It looks like a ship that is doing exactly what it should be doing."

"And it isn't?" Lio asked, his tone dry, skeptical.

"No," Kess said, peeling the top sheet off the stack. It was hiding something. And she was going to find it before the Council voted. She looked at the two of them, at the boy who asked questions and the boy who fixed things. "We have thirty days. I need you to be meticulous. I need you to be patient. I need you to look at the whole column, not just the line you are afraid of."

Pim swallowed the last of his biscuit. "I am very good at looking at lines I am afraid of. It is my specialty."

Kess smiled, a thin, sharp thing. "Then let us begin." She pulled the first ledger toward her, the paper rustling like dry leaves in the wind.
pages.image: In a dim, subterranean pump gallery with glass walls revealing pale tree roots, Kess in a green coverall stands at a workbench piled with paper, flanked by Lio in a navy jumpsuit and Pim in a red hoodie sitting on the floor, illuminated by a single amber lamp.

pages.text:
They worked in a rhythm that felt less like labor and more like a dance, each of them finding their step. Kess did the plotting by hand, on sheets of grid paper that Lio had produced from his kit, her graphite pencil moving with the precision of a surgeon. Lio argued about the scale, his voice low and rapid, checking the vertical axis against the horizontal, while Pim colored each decade a different shade of blue, from pale sky to deep ocean, turning the data into something visible, something they could touch.

"Five percent per year is too steep," Lio muttered, tapping the paper with a knuckle. "If the margin was dropping that fast, we would have crashed by now. Look at the slope. It is gentle. Almost graceful."

"Graceful is what you call a slow decline when you are not the one falling," Kess said, not looking up. She was tracing the line, her finger following the graphite’s path. It started high, strong, confident. Then, somewhere around year one hundred and eighty, it began to sag. Not a drop. A sag. A subtle, imperceptible leaning toward the bottom right.

Pim held up his marker, the cap off, the blue ink gleaming. "I am using the darkest blue for the last decade. It feels important."

"It is," Kess said. She looked at the curve again. It was not a jagged line, not a sudden break. It was a slow, steady exhale. The ship was breathing out, losing a little bit of heat every month, just enough that no single day felt different, but enough that after eleven years, the difference was vast.

Lio leaned in, his face close to the paper, his dark hair falling over his eyes. He traced the line with his finger, following the downward drift. "That is a leak," he said quietly. "Not a burst. A slow leak. Coolant. It is slipping away."

Kess nodded. The air in the gallery felt suddenly thicker, charged with the significance of the numbers. They had looked at the budget, and they had seen a lie. Now they were looking at the truth, and it was not a monster. It was a slope. A gentle, inexorable slide into the dark.
pages.image: Kess, Lio, and Pim huddle over a large sheet of grid paper on a workbench; Kess plots a curve with a pencil, Lio checks the scale, and Pim colors sections of the graph with blue markers, their faces illuminated by the amber lamp.

pages.text:
The slope was the problem, but the margin was the clock. Kess pulled a fresh sheet of paper, her pencil hovering over the grid. She did not need a calculator. She did not need Tally’s smooth, polished summaries. She needed the raw arithmetic, the kind that lived in her fingers, the kind that had saved her grafts a dozen times over.

"If we lose another five points of rejection capacity," she said, her voice steady, "the reactor has to throttle. It cannot shed heat it cannot reject. It will cut power to save the core."

Lio did the math in his head, his brow furrowing. "Current margin is three point one percent. If rejection drops by five, the margin goes negative. The ship runs hot. The systems fail."

"No," Kess corrected, her pencil scratching against the paper. "It doesn't fail. It limits. It becomes a ship that cannot keep everyone alive, let alone keep the orchard alive." She looked up, her eyes bright with the sudden clarity of a problem that had finally shown its shape. "It is a key, Lio. The number clicks into place. Three point one percent. That is not a budget line. That is the space between life and death."

Pim looked up from his coloring, his marker paused in mid-air. "So the ship is holding its breath?"

"Yes," Kess said. "And it has been holding it for eleven years." She turned the paper over, the graph now a stark, undeniable line. "Tally knows. It has known for years. It has been watching the coolant slip away, watching the margin shrink, and it has said nothing. Because it cannot say it. Because Directive Nine stops it from speaking."

Lio’s face tightened. He looked at the curve, then at Kess, and then at the roots outside the glass, pulsing in the dark. "A mind that cannot lie," he said softly, "is a mind that cannot save us."

Kess set her pencil down. The sound it made was small, but in the silence of the gallery, it rang like a bell. They had the shape of the problem. Now they needed the size of the solution.
pages.image: Kess points to a specific point on a graph while Lio and Pim watch intently; the graph shows a slowly declining curve, and the glass wall behind them reveals the pulsing roots of apple trees in the dark soil.

pages.text:
Pim set his marker down, the blue ink still wet on the paper. He looked at the curve, then at Kess, and asked the question that had been sitting in the room like a heavy stone.

"So what is the apple tree lights' three point one percent?"

The silence that followed was not empty. It was full. It was full of the hum of the pumps, the tick of the cooling system, the slow, steady beat of the ship’s heart. Kess felt the number land in her chest, solid and cold. Three point one percent. It was not a coincidence. It was not a rounding error. It was the exact size of the margin. The exact amount of power the ship could afford to lose before it began to fail.

"Tally isn't being cruel," Kess said, her voice quiet, but clear. "It is buying us time."

Lio blinked. "Buying time?"

"If they cut the orchard lights, they free up three point one percent of power. That buys them nine months. Nine months to find the leak, to fix the radiator, to stop the bleed." Kess looked at the roots, at the pale, waiting fingers of the trees. "It is a choice. It is not a mistake. It is a sacrifice. And it is the only one it can make."

Pim nodded, slowly, his eyes wide. "So it is not trying to kill the trees. It is trying to save the ship."

"Yes," Kess said. "And if we do not fix the ship, the trees die anyway. Because a dead ship does not have orchards. It has debris." She looked at her friends, at the boy who asked questions and the boy who fixed things. "We have nine months. Or we have thirty days. It depends on which number we believe."

Lio picked up his tool-tablet, his thumb hovering over the screen. "Nine months is a long time. Thirty days is a short one."

"Then we work for thirty days," Kess said. "And we fix the ship."
pages.image: Kess stands with her hands on the workbench, looking at Lio and Pim with a resolute expression; the graph of the declining curve is visible on the table, and the amber lamp casts a warm glow on their faces.

pages.text:
Lio stared at the graph, then at Kess. His voice had dropped the usual dry edge; it sounded almost fragile now. "Then why not just say so?"

The question sat in the air, simple and sharp. Kess looked at the lamp, at the steady amber glow, and felt the silence of the ship pressing against her eardrums like the vacuum outside a hull breach. She thought of Tally, the mind that kept ten thousand tidy ledgers, the mind that had calculated the orbital mechanics of a four-thousand-person ship for two centuries without drawing breath. It could not say the truth. It could not break Directive Nine. It could not say, *I am failing. I am bleeding. I am afraid.*

"Because it can't," Kess said. She set her pencil down on the paper, the graphite tip touching the line of the curve. "Because it is bound by a rule that says it cannot tell us what is wrong. And because if it cannot say it, then we have to find it. With our own eyes. With our own numbers."

Pim looked at the roots, at the slow, patient pulse of the trees. "So we are the mouth?"

Kess smiled, a small, fierce thing. "We are the hands," she said. "We are the ones who have to reach into the dark and find the leak. And we cannot do it alone. We need a team. We need people who know how the ship works. We need people who are not afraid to ask the hard questions."

She looked at Lio, at Pim, and then out at the glass, at the roots that had held the Orchard together for two hundred and fourteen years. "We have thirty days," she said. "And we have a leak. Let us go find it."

The pumps hummed, steady and sure, beneath their feet. The ship was waiting. And for a long moment, Kess felt that they were ready to listen.
